title: Six tastes of a new year

card.keepWhy: Sweet and bitter in one spoon, and yes to both.
sources: Ugadi, the new year for many Hindus in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, on the first day of the bright half of Chaitra

Ugadi pachadi: jaggery, tamarind, neem flowers, salt, green chili or black pepper, raw mango (six tastes), commonly paired with happiness, disgust, sadness, fear, anger and surprise, the mixed experiences of the year ahead
Even-mindedness in joy and sorrow: Bhagavad Gita 2.38; Rama’s steady face (week two)

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you start something new, do you hope it’ll be all good? then something bitter shows up.

steps.line: On Ugadi, the new year for many Hindus in South India, families eat a little dish called pachadi.
It has six tastes in one spoon.

steps.q: It’s a happy festival dish. Do you guess any of the six tastes is bitter?
o: No, all six are pleasant, for a happy year
Bitter, but only in the elders’ spoons
steps.why: Bitter too, on purpose. Watch why.

steps.line: Sweet jaggery, sour tamarind, bitter neem flowers, salt, spicy chili, and tangy raw mango.

steps.q: Ugadi’s name joins two Sanskrit words, yuga and adi. What does it mean?
steps.why: Yuga, an age; adi, a beginning. Many tellings say it marks the day Brahma began creating the world.

steps.line: The meaning is simple. The new year will bring all six.

steps.pre: In many homes, each taste stands for a feeling. The bitter neem stands for
steps.why: Neem is sorrow. In the usual telling, chili is anger, salt is fear, tamarind is disgust, raw mango is surprise, and jaggery is joy.

steps.line: Joy and sadness, anger and fear, surprise and disgust. Eat them all at once, and accept them all.

steps.q: Why would a festival dish include something bitter on purpose?
o: Bitter food was thought to bring luck
To say yes to the hard parts too
steps.why: The new year won’t be all sweet. Tasting the bitter with family is a way to say yes to the whole year; many also say neem guards health as the hot season starts.

steps.line: A real fresh start makes room for the bitter, and the sweet.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. ugadi doesn’t promise a perfect year. it hands you the whole year in one spoon.
hindu teaching prizes an even heart, meeting joy and sorrow alike, the way rama met crown and forest. pachadi lets you practice it with your tongue.

steps.q: Someone takes their spoon of pachadi and carefully picks out the neem flowers. From the lesson, what are they missing?
o: The best flavor in the whole dish
The point: taking bitter with sweet
Nothing, since the bitter is optional
steps.why: Pachadi is never all sweet. Picking out the bitter is like asking for a year with no hard days.

today.say: name one sweet thing and one bitter thing you expect this month. say yes to both. many families begin ugadi with a prayer and the pachadi together. you can join in, learn more, or just taste the idea. it’s your choice.
options: then that’s your pachadi. one spoon.
then hold on. the sweet is in the spoon too.
